Hypotension after an endovascular procedure should always include retroperitoneal bleeding in the differential; lower abdominal or flank pain and an acute hematocrit drop suggest it; a high puncture above the inguinal ligament is the main risk; confirmed by CT of the abdomen and pelvis; stable patients: transfusion, heparin reversal with protamine and close blood pressure monitoring; unstable patients: volume resuscitation and urgent angiography from the other side, with balloon, covered stent or surgery. handover: NSTEMI. One drug-eluting stent at 14:00 through a 6 French right femoral sheath; heparin during the case. Sheath pulled at 16:30 with 20 minutes of manual pressure. Aspirin and ticagrelor.
16:30: heart rate 72, blood pressure 134/78, hemoglobin 13.4 this morning, type and screen sent at 18:00. Groin checks every 15 minutes have been clean.

Post-procedure standing orders: bed rest flat for 4 hours; 500 mL lactated Ringer's bolus for hypotension or signs of bleeding, then call the interventional fellow; stat hemoglobin and type and crossmatch by protocol.

cues.question: What do you think is happening to Mr. Adeyemi, why might the groin look normal, and why act before the hemoglobin comes back?

parts.label: What and why
parts.criteria: Names a retroperitoneal bleed from the femoral puncture: new back or flank pain, restlessness and a rising heart rate with a drifting pressure after a femoral procedure on antiplatelet drugs and heparin; explains that a high puncture bleeds behind the inguinal ligament where nothing shows at the groin.
parts.modelAnswer: Back and flank pain, restlessness, a heart rate up from 72 to the high 80s and a pressure drifting down, four hours after a femoral PCI on aspirin, ticagrelor and heparin, is a retroperitoneal bleed until proved otherwise. A puncture above the inguinal ligament bleeds into the retroperitoneum, so the groin can look perfect while liters collect behind it.

parts.label: Why not wait
parts.criteria: Explains that the first hemoglobin lags behind acute loss and that compensation hides the volume lost until the pressure falls; acts now: flat, pressure above the puncture, a bolus, SBAR to the interventional team naming the bleed, blood when ready, imaging or angiography; no opioid in place of escalation.
parts.modelAnswer: His hemoglobin will barely move at first because he is losing whole blood, and his heart rate is compensating; by the time the pressure falls he has lost a large share of his volume. So: flat with the leg straight, firm pressure above the puncture, a bolus by the standing order, a stat hemoglobin and crossmatch, and an SBAR to the fellow that names a retroperitoneal bleed. Then blood as soon as it arrives and angiography or CT. Morphine for the pain without telling anyone would hide the warning.

expertPath.text: Assess: flank and back pain, restless, heart rate up, pressure drifting; groin soft with no hematoma, pulses intact. Flat with the leg straight, pressure above the puncture, bolus started, stat hemoglobin and crossmatch drawn.

arrest.headline: Arrest from a hidden bleed
arrest.body: The groin looked fine because the blood went behind it. New back or flank pain with a rising heart rate after a femoral procedure needs pressure, volume and a call that names the bleed, not a wait for the hemoglobin.

labTarget.headline: Recognized and acted on before the hemoglobin
labTarget.body: Pressure above the puncture, flat, a bolus, an SBAR that named a retroperitoneal bleed, blood as soon as it came and angiography while he was still perfused. That is the expert path.

labLate.headline: To angiography, by a slower route
labLate.body: He reached angiography, but check how soon the bleed was named, whether pressure and fluids started early, whether blood waited, and whether the pain was treated before anyone was told.

time_up.headline: Still bleeding at 20:40
time_up.body: No one put the flank pain together with the heart rate and the pressure, so the interventional team never came. A normal-looking groin does not rule out a retroperitoneal bleed.

scoring.modelReasoning: Back and flank pain, restlessness, a heart rate climbing from 72 and a pressure drifting down four hours after a femoral PCI on aspirin, ticagrelor and heparin is a retroperitoneal bleed until proved otherwise, even with a clean groin: a puncture above the inguinal ligament bleeds into the retroperitoneum. The first hemoglobin lags behind acute loss and the heart rate hides the deficit, so act before the result: keep him flat with the leg straight, hold firm pressure over the artery about an inch above the skin puncture, start the standing-order bolus, draw a stat hemoglobin and crossmatch, and call the interventional fellow with an SBAR that names the bleed. Give blood as soon as it arrives (the restrictive thresholds are for stable patients) and get him to imaging or angiography while he is still perfused. An opioid for the pain without escalation hides the warning.

hgbQ.ask: The first hemoglobin may come back close to this morning's. What does that tell you?

choices.label: That he is not bleeding much
Little: hemoglobin lags behind acute blood loss, so it is repeated

hgbQ.explain: Whole blood is lost at the same concentration, so the number barely moves at first; it falls as fluid refills the vessels and as crystalloid runs in. Act on the trend in his vital signs and his symptoms, and repeat the hemoglobin.

groinQ.ask: His groin is soft with no hematoma. Does that make a bleed unlikely?

No: a puncture above the inguinal ligament bleeds into the retroperitoneum, out of sight

groinQ.explain: A high puncture bleeds backward into the retroperitoneal space, where there is room for liters of blood and nothing shows at the groin. Back, flank or lower abdominal pain with a rising heart rate and a falling pressure after a femoral procedure is a retroperitoneal bleed until proved otherwise.
